articles.text: The Piedmont Community Band may not have been the largest or loudest marching band in the Fourth of July Parade, but they may have had the most fun. This year saw several new players, a sign of the band’s success at staying together and evolving over the past 40 years. The band was founded by Jane Reed, who still plays alto sax and serves as co-director with Greg Slatoff. The marching musical group’s Sergeant Major is bass drum player and PHS alumnus Rachel Bloom, who sets the pace and keeps the band of 20–25 musicians tight in formation and tune. articles.text: Editor: As a 33 year-long Piedmont resident in Sidney and Irene Dearing’s neighborhood, I vehemently oppose the design and installation of this permanent public memorial for them. Why was the neighborhood never consulted about it? I do applaud honoring the Dearings, maybe in an effort to atone for the misdeeds of Piedmonters of the past, however, this work of art is no way in harmony with the character of our neighborhood, or this beautiful city we live in. The proposed design would do well in modern cities such as Brasilia or Dubai, but clearly not here. I doubt the Dearings would enjoy looking at it, defacing this little gem of a park, and upsetting its magnificent redwoods.. Because this creative artist has cleverly designed these statement pieces with enclosed benches, trash will accumulate within the sculptures. In addition, the walls made with wood, with attract vandalism, such as graffiti. The structures will require quite a bit of maintenance, and painting over the years. A beautiful bronze plaque, telling the story, would be infinitely more appropriate. Neighborly Yours, Dr. Jean-Pierre L. articles.text: Zeppelin is a sweet, scruffy teddy bear of a dog, who is about 2.5 years old and 56 lovable pounds (working on that weight loss journey!). This guy has a playful side and is good at making dog friends in playgroups and in his foster home. He can be shy on first meetings, but he quickly warms up when people are patient and can offer tasty treats. Zeppelin knows sit, down, and shake, and absolutely loves couch cuddles. articles.text: Let’s be real: If I’m starving and exhausted on a Wednesday night, I will 100% grab that frozen burrito out of the freezer and call it dinner. But would I call it good? Not exactly. Now imagine a different kind of meal. One where you take your time browsing the local farmers market, choosing tomatoes that feel just right, chatting with the sourdough guy — maybe even planning your menu based on what looks and smells the freshest. You get home, put on music, chop, stir, simmer. The scent fills your kitchen, and when you sit down to eat, it’s not just a meal — it’s an experience. That’s slow food. And it’s not just about what you eat; it’s about how you make it. Here’s the thing: Creativity works the same way. In the age of AI, we’re all standing in the metaphorical freezer aisle. You want a poem? A song? A logo? A painting? A marketing campaign? AI can crank it out in seconds. And just like that frozen burrito, it might do the job. But if we rely only on the fast, easy version, we lose something essential: the process. Creativity isn’t just about the final product — it’s about what happens in your brain (and your heart) when you take the long way. When you doodle without a plan. When you write a story, then rewrite it, then throw it away and start over. When you try to paint the sunset and realize halfway through that it looks more like a lopsided pumpkin — but keep going anyway. Just like slow food, slow creativity feeds us in a different way. It keeps the curious, nonlinear, playful parts of our minds alive. It teaches us patience and perseverance. It helps us make meaning — not just output. AI is here to stay, and it’s a powerful tool. But if we only use it as a shortcut, we risk turning the most human parts of ourselves into frozen meals. Efficient? Yes. Predictable? Sure. But kind of bland — and definitely not inspiring. So let’s start a movement. Call it From Scratch. Call it Slow Made. Call it Brain to Page. Call it whatever you want. But the next time you sit down to make something, pause for a moment. Give yourself permission to linger. To explore. To savor the process. Because that’s where the flavor is. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in the 3Cs: Creativity, Communication and Connection. https://ninameehan. com/

The Piedmont Fencing Team recently traveled to Milwaukee, Wisconsin for the 2025 National Championships hosted by USA Fencing. Summer Nationals are considered as a marquee event for youth fencers, with 6,000 competitors from across the country. Representing Piedmont was rising PHS freshman Maya Dvoiris and elementary student Ian Stock. Dvoiris competed in the Cadet Women’s Foil and Youth 14 Women’s Foil categories, while Stock was in the Youth 10 Men’s Foil event. Dvoiris finished 176th of 262 athletes in the Cadet Women’s Foil and 217th of 299 in the Youth 14 Women’s Foil. She reached the Tableau knockout stages in both events. In the Cadet Women’s Foil pool play, Dvoiris opened with a 5-3 win over Olivia Chang of Golubitsky Fencing in Orange County and followed up with a 5-3 victory over Mia Bertolini of Marx Fencing in Massachusetts. She followed with four losses, but had close 5-3 defeats to Reese Samala of Cleveland Fencing Academy and Annika Krahe of Brooklyn Bridge Fencing Club. Maya moved onto the tableau stage with the 174th seed and faced No. 81 Haley Pedersen of United Fencing Academy, losing 15-9. In the Y-14 Women’s Foil, Dvoiris won two of six matches. She dominated Kenzie Lin of Renaissance Fencing in Michigan 5-1 and followed with a 5-4 win over Pelu Akinbamiro of Fort Bend Fencing in Houston. She had a narrow 5-4 loss to Zoya Baulin of Manhattan Fencing Club. She faced No. 39 Maya Photos courtesy of Piedmont Fencing Team Orbe-Austin of Peter Westbrook Fencing in New York after receiving the No. 217 seed. Dvoiris played her opponent close to a 12-7 loss. Stock won one of his six matches, a victory that came in dominant fashion with a 5-1 drubbing of Ben Brown of Fioretto Fencing Academy in Florida. Among his losses was a narrow 5-4 battle against Lionel Fang of Mid Island Fencing Academy in New York. He received the No. 138 seed in the tableau and faced Zhengxuan Lin of Bay Area Fencing Club in Los Gatos, losing in a 10-6 contest. articles.text: Coach Jordan Seiden gathers the football team at the Lake Tahoe Football Camp. Piedmont High’s football team recently traveled to South Lake Tahoe for the Lake Tahoe Football Camp June 16-19 at Lake Tahoe Community College. The response was strong with 39 players from varsity and junior varsity rosters. Piedmont competed with 15 other schools in 7-on-7, 11-on-11, and in an offensive line vs. defensive line event called “Trench Wars.” “It was great for the kids to get a week together,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We were the smallest team, but the boys really went up there and competed. We grew a lot and saw areas that we need to work on. We had our ups and downs, and we expected that. It’s early in the summer, so we only have so many plays installed.” Head track coach Pouyan Assadi, a varsity assistant, also made the trip. “The 72 hours we were in Tahoe, I genuinely believe was 4-6 weeks of practice crammed into one,” Assadi said. “There were 16 individual teams that, including teams from Wyoming, Idaho, and Nevada. This is the place you want to go if your team wants to get better.” The camp gave coach Seiden to take a look at his roster ahead of 2025 season, when the Highlanders will undergo vast changes. They lost a total of 16 seniors from last year’s WACC Mission Division title-winning team. The only returning fulltime two-way starter is offensive and defensive lineman Adrian Kondakov. “One of the biggest things about the offensive line is continuity. That group has to work together and they did well. Adrian is our leader and just goes out there and gets it done. He’s like a bear pushing his cubs to where they need to go. He’s really stepped up all summer. We’re going to have four new starters, and Adrian is the only player back who was a full-time starter,” Seiden said. The camp offered sophomore Jimmy Lagios, the younger brother of three-year starting quarterback Markos Lagios, and opportunity to show his skills. Returning to potentially making an impact to their offense is Xavier Henderson and Rehan Mumtaz. Piedmont earned five AllCamp honors, including Lagios, Kondakov, and offensive and defensive lineman Chase Knapp in the varsity level, and quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster and tight end and linebacker Mason Gray in the junior varsity level. “Jimmy did really well; he was great. Guys are going to get a lot of reps, so we need to make sure everyone can handle that. We came back healthy and will get Photos by JC Curran back to work this week,” Seiden said. The Highlanders will continue with their own training camp through the summer until the start of padded practice in mid-August. “These are the dog days of the summer. It’s grinding, paying attention to detail, and spending a lot of time in the weight room. We need to get our bodies ready to go,” Seiden said. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s football team recently traveled to South Lake Tahoe for the Lake Tahoe Football Camp June 16-19 at Lake Tahoe Community College. The response was strong with 39 players from varsity and junior varsity rosters. Piedmont competed with 15 other schools in 7-on-7, 11-on-11, and in an offensive line vs. defensive line event called “Trench Wars.” “It was great for the kids to get a week together,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We were the smallest team, but the boys really went up there and competed. We grew a lot and saw areas that we need to work on. We had our ups and downs, and we expected that. articles.text: The chamber music festival Music in the Vineyards kicks off its 31st season in Napa Valley on August 1. The series of live performances traditionally showcases distinguished chamber musicians as well emerging young talent during its four-week season, with concerts held at popular wineries and vineyards throughout the valley. This year’s featured artists include the Borromeo String Quartet, Pacifica Quartet and Ariel Quartet, as well as Pavone String Quartet, a group of undergraduate students at the world-renowned Shepherd School of Music at Rice University. The Pavone Quartet is winner of Music in the Vineyards’ 2025 Fellowship Quartet competition and will perform on August 11. Since the festival’s inception in 1995, wineries in Napa Valley continue to lend their space for MITV musicians to perform live, offering a uniquely Northern Californian festival experience. With complimentary wine tastings at each intermission and breathtaking views of the Napa Valley, this unique combination of wine country ambiance and great musicianship allows audiences to experience chamber music in small intimate settings. Music venues this year include Clos Pegase Winery, Frog’s Leap Winery, Hess Persson Estates, Domaine Carneros, Louis M. Martini Winery, Maxville Winery, Stag’s Leap Wine Cellars, Hudson Ranch, Ehlers Estate, Markham Vineyards, Hudson House at Beringer Vineyards, Spottswoode Estate, Silverado Vineyards, and Inglenook. articles.text: Korsa Musical Theater, a Bay Area musical theater training company, concludes its 20th season with a production of Oklahoma! showing July 18 through 27 at the Pinole Valley High School Theater. Oklahoma! is the first musical written by Rodgers and Hammerstein, a theater-writing team of composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist-dramatist Oscar Hammerstein II. The 1943 musical is based on Lynn Riggs’s 1931 play Green Grow the Lilacs and follows the story of farmgirl Laurey and cowboy Curly’s budding romance, threatened by a brooding ranch-hand named Jud. The play ran for over five years on Broadway, a record that would not be bested until My Fair Lady’s initial run in 1956. Korsa Musical Theater’s production features a cast of 33 student performers age 13 through 20, led by a team of professional directors including award-winning Director Susannah Martin, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Janet Collard. The production also includes a 30-piece live orchestra, with five student instrumentalists playing Robert Russell Bennet’s original score. The run consists of four 7 p.m. performances on July 18, 19, 25, and 26; and two 2:00 p.m. matinees on July 20 and 28. Tickets are available online at www.korsamt.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $18–$40, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. Pinole Valley High School Theater is located at 2900 Pinole Valley Road in Pinole. Photography by Jonah Pagenhart Evie Mitchell and Maddox Scardina in Korsa Musical Theater’s Oklahoma!

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes former artist-in-residence Angelique Kidjo and world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma to UC Berkeley’s historic Greek Theatre in a special Labor Day weekend performance on Saturday, August 30. Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and has earned recognition over the years for projects like Yemandja, the artist’s first major foray into stage acting, and a reboot of the Talking Heads’ classic 1980 album Remain in Light, both part of the Cal Performances 2021–22 season. The Benin-born singer was also named one of Time magazine’s “100 Most Influential People of 2021” for her work as a performer, teacher, and cultural ambassador. Her latest recordings incorporate West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music, and remains one of the world’s most well-respected cellists. The Labor Day concert is Cellist Yo-Yo Ma with Angelique Kidjo part of Cal Performances’ Illuminations: “Exile & Sanctuary” programming for the 2025–26 season, a theme that aims to “connect seven unique performances to academic research” on the UC Berkeley campus, focusing on physical displacement, rupture of identity, and “a stripping away of the familiar that leaves an individual or community without a sense of belonging.” The performance connects centuries of interaction between African musical idioms and western music, highlighting exile and sanctuary as both a refuge and a creative space for artists. Ma and Kidjo use the Baroque sarabande dance form and its possible African antecedent, a dance to worship the Congolese spirit Zarabanda as a method to showcase the qualities that connect different cultures, genres, and musical traditions. “Every day there are moments when all of us can feel we are on the inside of something and also when we feel we are on the outside of something,” Ma said in a statement. “To be able to understand both at the same time and oscillate between the two gives us a larger perspective on the world.” “If your mind is open, and there is no fear, it’s easier to listen, and to question yourself,” Kidjo added. Tickets are likely to sell out fast. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances. org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m.

articles.text: Materialized Thoughts, an art exhibit coming to the Piedmont Center for the Arts, brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life—particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. These artworks investigate the nuanced realities of diasporic life – living in between cultures, constantly navigating the differences and similarities between homeland and host land, and the ongoing process of carving out a new identity. This exhibition is the culmination of the research on Nepali Diaspora Artists based in the Bay Area and beyond, conducted by Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha as a Fulbright Visiting Scholar, 2024- 25, with the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco. The research was conducted over seven months in 2024-2025. This exhibition is the first of its kind, featuring artworks selectively by Diaspora Nepali Artists, showcasing diverse cultural narratives, challenging dominant art world narratives, and fostering dialogue about identity, displacement, and belonging. This exhibition has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities, seeking to play a crucial role in cultural preservation, documentation of history, and promoting cross-cultural understanding. Through such exhibitions by diaspora artists, you can help gain a deeper understanding of cultural identity, witness artistic innovation, and engage with important social issues. They also foster empathy and understanding of shared human experiences, challenges, and triumphs, providing an opportunity to celebrate the diversity of artistic talent and contribute to a more inclusive art world. Supporting diaspora artists can contribute to a more inclusive and globally oriented art world, enriching the cultural landscape and contribute to a broader understanding of the diaspora’s impact on contemporary culture and society.

articles.text: World-renowned classical guitarist Derek Gripper from South Africa is set to play at the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) on July 12. After quickly selling out of tickets for his 8:00 p.m., a 5:30p.m. show was added. Tickets are selling fast, with the classically-trained musician on the verge of becoming PCA’s first ever double-sold-out show. Gripper is a guitarist and composer renowned for his unique ability to transcribe and perform complex West African kora music on the classical guitar. His work bridges the gap between different musical traditions and has garnered international recognition for its innovation and virtuosity. Gripper gained widespread attention from his ability to translate arrangements from the African kora, a 21-string harp, featured on his 2012 album One Night on Earth, a recording so unexpected that celebrated guitarist John Williams said, “It seemed absolutely impossible until I heard Derek Gripper do it.” Gripper said his project was about creating previously unseen connection between African oral traditions and Western classical music, bridging the gap between different ways of listening and understanding. Along the way, Gripper has performed with legendary musicians like John Williams and Toumani Diabaté’s Symmetric Orchestra, sharing stages from Carnegie Hall to Shakespeare’s Globe. The journey from kora to guitar came full circle last year, when Gripper partnered with kora legend Ballaké Sissoko on a joint tour and album. Though the two musicians did not share a language, they were able to play music together with beautiful improvisation. No two shows on that tour were alike, but their 2024 album Ballaké Sissoko & Derek Gripper remains for music lovers to enjoy. “It was a very natural project – we just had to sit together,” explained Gripper. “…It’s a project that was done very much in the moment. articles.text: Cary Grant in the iconic scene from Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest I would suggest that each of Alfred Hitchcock’s films, to include North By Northwest, is a master class in taut, well-plotted, compelling storytelling and often mirror the noir genre of the 1940s (e.g. Double Indemnity, The Big Sleep). Vertigo, Rear Window and, of course, the breathtaking Psycho are only a few examples of this auteur’s years of filmmaking. NXNW opens with Roger Thornhill (Cary Grant) having lunch with business associates in a white tablecloth New York restaurant. He is unexpectedly paged, excuses himself, and finds that there are two men waiting for him who refer to him as a Mr. Kaplan. Trying to explain that his name is Thornhill not Kaplan, he is nevertheless roughly escorted from the restaurant and shoved into a waiting car. Ignoring his protests, he is driven to a mansion where he is taken inside and told to wait in the library. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Only Yesterday Only Yesterday was written and directed by Isao Takahata who cofounded the remarkable Studio Ghibli with Hayao Miyazaki. When released in Japan in 1991, it was a box office sensation, yet, surprisingly, failed to reach the U.S. until 2016. If the works of Miyazaki and Takahata have captured the imaginations of your youngsters, then Only Yesterday is a must see. It’s extraordinary, an example, once again, of the stunning artistry and story telling that has become the brand of Ghibli. The film’s narrative touches on adult themes while focusing on a hybrid protagonist: a 27-year-old woman and a 10-year-old girl. The story begins with Taeko Okajima (Daisey Ridley), a kind of Japanese everywoman, an office worker and life-long resident of Tokyo. She departs by train for a vacation trip in the country to visit relatives, intending to help with the seasonal harvest of safflowers. On her journey, while travelling through the night on a sleeper car, headed for the rural town of Yamagata, she begins to reminisce about her childhood: a strict father, puberty, bad grades, first crushes, insecurities, the mockery of mean girls, all told from the point-of- view of a 10-year-old who is negotiating the 5th grade. These images, beautifully animated, lyrical, and are blended seamlessly with the reactions of the older, increasingly reflective Taeko. At one point she says, “I didn’t expect to bring my fifth-grade self along for the trip.” She is met at the Yamagata train station by a young man, Toshio (Dev Patel), a friend of the family, with whom she strikes up a friendship and it’s with him that she begins to share her very personal and conflicted memories. During her stay in this bucolic setting, walking the fields of flowers, enveloped by the soft hillsides, she grows ever more wistful about her past. She reflects on her dreams from childhood, her hopes and dreams, some splashed, and wonders if the life she is living in Tokyo is truly one she wishes to continue. And there is, of course, her growing fondness for Toshio. Only Yesterday is a work of art, wonderfully told, absent intensely imagined, suspend-your-disbelief characters. Instead, the fable moves gently, at times sadly, from the present to the past and back with calm tenderness. Only Yesterday. Written and directed by Isao Takahata. Animé by Studio Ghibli. With voices of Daisy Ridley, Dev Patel and Ashley Eckstein. 1 hr. 58 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019. Streaming on MAX/Roku/apple tv/Prime/ Fandango/Hulu

articles.text: Captain America: The First Avenger is, at least initially, set in New York City. The year is 1942. Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and his best friend, Sgt. Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), are downtown attending a future technology exhibition, and happen to pass a military recruitment station. War is in the air, Bucky is about to ship out for Europe, and countless men are enlisting, with the exception of Steve who suffers from asthma, and weighs in at some 98 pounds. It’s not for trying that he’s not in uniform, and to his chagrin he’s been rejected multiple times. As it happens, also attending the exhibition is Dr. Abraham Erskine (Stanley Rucci), a brilliant inventor and genetic scientist, working on a special “super soldier” experiment for the Strategic Scientific Reserve. The project is under the command of Col. Chester Phillips (Tommy Lee Jones). Dr. Erskine happens to overhear a conversation of regret between Bucky and Steve, and looking at the scrawny Steve decides he might be perfect for his special serum and what are referred to as “vita rays.” Pulling a few strings with Col. Phillips, the scientist manages to get Steve into the program. Ever hopeful, willing to try anything to enlist, he agrees. Stretched out on a table, machinery begins to hum and spark, the serum/vita rays are administered, and to his Chris Evans in Captain America: The First Avenger surprise, Steve emerges much taller, more muscular, with an ability to now run at a tremendous speed. In other words, he has been indeed transformed into a super soldier. Amazing at the result, the army decides to dress him in stars and striped tights, hood, provide him with a shield and send him cross-country to advertise for war bonds using the name Captain America. The best part of Captain America: The first Avenger is the transformation of weakling Steve Rogers into his alter ego: he’s now a square-jawed, humble, even shy superhero who soon is sent out to fight for truth, justice, and the American way. Soon he confronts his uber-nemesis and Nazi provocateur, the villainous, megalomaniac Red Skull (Hugo Weaving) and his army of thugs called Hydra, all ensconced in Red Skull’s alpine forest retreat where he is conducting his own experiment: a blue-cube that will enable him to take over the world. Of course, the story – a big, bold, razzle-dazzle adventure – has plenty of action, chase scenes, shootouts, a submarine, aircraft, and even a fight on top of a Nazi blimp, all leading to a spectacular showdown between Captain America and Red Skull. And there’s even a touch of romance between MI 16 Brit spy, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), who has been assigned to the Strategic Reserve. Kids will love this origin film, one that will soon be followed by The Avengers, introducing lots of superheroes. Stay tuned. Captain America: The First Avenger, Directed by Joe Johnson. Starring Chris Evans, Hayley Atwell, Hugo Weaving. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Streaming on Fandango/ Prime/Disney+/apple tv.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group met at the Exedra on Wednesday, July 2, to enjoy an early summer walk together on a lovely morning. With the Fourth of July just two days away, the group was already getting into the spirit. There was an excellent holiday-week turnout of 42 walkers — and four K-9 best friends. The group welcomed Charlie, along with Lynn and Dave Holzman, who brought Pepper and Fiona for their first walk with the group. Before the usual 10:30 a.m. start, Peggy Shultz, a physical therapist, led a helpful refresher on fall prevention and safe walking exercises. As the group gathered, someone pointed out a fun fact: July 2 was the 183rd day of the year in the Gregorian calendar, meaning 182 days remained — it was the halfway point of the year. With noon being the group’s typical finish time, they could officially celebrate a “Happy New Half Year.” The group was also reminded that they’d soon be walking in the Fourth of July Parade — and a bit of Piedmont parade history was shared. The city’s first official parade took place 60 years ago, in 1965, thanks to Dick Johnson, then-chairman of the Recreation Commission. Johnson’s El Cerrito Avenue neighborhood had already been celebrating Independence Day since the mid-1950s with its own kids’ bike parade, watermelon-eating contest, and water balloon toss. Mary Ellen Sherry and Dorothy Carter, who lived on the block, had taken part in similar festivities elsewhere and wanted the same for their street. Alongside neighbors like Dick Carter and Patty Edmonds, they created the El Cerrito event. Johnson pushed to expand it citywide, giving rise to the Piedmont parade we know today. In honor of that legacy, the walkers headed to El Cerrito Avenue to see where it all began. From there, they made their way to Mesa Avenue, where they would gather on Friday to join the parade. Nearby, they paused to spot a local treasure — a pair of bald eagles and their two eaglets nesting in a eucalyptus tree at the edge of Mountain View Cemetery. The eaglets had hatched in May and were first spotted by the group in early June. Since eaglets typically don’t fledge for 10 to 14 weeks, the birds were still at home — and the walkers hoped for another look. Along the way, they stopped at the under-construction aquatics center on Magnolia Avenue, where cement was being poured and the site was buzzing with activity. The walkers continued to the 300 block of El Cerrito — the birthplace of Piedmont’s first July 4 street celebration nearly 70 years ago — then crossed Oakland Avenue to Blair Avenue, up Dracena Avenue, and across to Park Way. Climbing Park past Highland, they arrived at 22 Mesa Avenue for a group photo. Before heading toward the eagle’s nest, a bit of ornithological trivia was shared: the bald eagle became the symbol of the United States when it was chosen for the Great Seal in 1782. articles.text: When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
